summary:
Lambayeque has no trans-specific ordinance, municipal rule or documented pattern of local enforcement on record; a trans visitor in this department is bound throughout by Peru's national framework.

The national framework restricts public restroom access. The Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity on 20 February 2025 a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting entry into public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to one's birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs; the article notes the text still needed plenary backing and reports the trigger as a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argues the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The IDEHPUCP institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms, including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI, and notes that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive.

Violence against trans people is documented at the national level. Peru recorded 54 assassinations of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in 2020-2023 according to the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian, with 19 killings in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women. Killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of 19 in 2023. In February 2023 trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano (31) was kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco (30) was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. These are national figures; the source provides no Lambayeque-specific breakdown, and the counts are raw totals without per-capita denominators.
tangentialFactors:
The national restroom restriction's enforcement mechanism, as described by activist Gianna Camacho, would rest on security staff checking the DNI to determine whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender, a check that could occur in any venue in Lambayeque subject to the law.

Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, per IDEHPUCP, which bears on how readily a trans visitor's documents will reflect their gender while in the department.

The national violence statistics are raw counts across all of Peru for 2020-2023 with no per-capita or regional breakdown, so they cannot be read as a Lambayeque-specific rate; the source inventory contains no Lambayeque-specific incident data.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Lambayeque are subject to the same national facility restriction as visitors: Article 5.1 of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes, approved by Congress's plenary on 2 April 2025, bars entry into public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than one's birth sex.

Discrimination complaints of this kind have been adjudicated through INDECOPI: SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's complaint against SmartFit over bathroom assignment based on DNI-recorded sex, indicating the administrative route available to residents has produced an adverse outcome in a documented case.

The state's crime-registration systems do not incorporate sexual orientation or gender identity, so hate-motivated violence against trans residents cannot be prosecuted as a hate crime.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Lambayeque-specific ordinance, municipal rule, enforcement incident, or local violence figure appears in the source inventory; the department's assessment rests entirely on the national framework, and any local practice by Chiclayo or provincial authorities is unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory does not state whether the 20 February 2025 dictamen and the 2 April 2025 plenary approval are the same legislative instrument or two steps in one process; both are reported as approved, and the final promulgation status of the merged text is not sourced.

Whether Lambayeque's health facilities, police units or courts have applied the national restroom restriction, or the DNI-check practice described by Gianna Camacho, is not documented in the inventory and remains unresolved.
